t:
(a) In General.—Section 1065 of title 10, United States Code, as added by section 621 of the John S. McCain National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2019 (Public Law 115–232), is amended—
        (1) in the heading, by striking “veterans and caregivers for veterans” and inserting “veterans, caregivers for veterans, and Foreign Service officers”; 
        (2) by redesignating subsections (f) and (g) as subsections (g) and (h), respectively; 
        (3) by inserting after subsection (e) the following new subsection (f):“(f) Eligibility of Foreign Service Officers on Mandatory Home Leave.—A Foreign Service officer on mandatory home leave 
may be permitted to use military lodging referred to in subsection (h).”; and 
        (4) in subsection (h), as redesignated by paragraph (2), by adding at the end the following new paragraphs:“(5) The term ‘Foreign Service officer’ has the meaning given that term in section 103 of the Foreign Service Act of 1980 (22 U.S.C. 3903).“(6) The term ‘mandatory home leave’ means leave under section 903 of the Foreign Service Act of 1980 (22 U.S.C. 4083).”.  
    (b) Effective Date.—The amendments made by this section shall take effect on January 1, 2020, as if originally incorporated in section 621 of Public Law 115–232.

fable.w: The section only extends eligibility for military lodging to Foreign Service officers on mandatory home leave and adds definitions and an effective date. The tempting reading is that "may be permitted" signals a decision process involving others, but Foreign Service officers are federal employees and this is a benefit eligibility provision. There is no consultation, comment period, hearing, advisory body, rulemaking, or right to sue involving anyone outside the federal government.
fable.s: may be permitted to use military lodging referred to in subsection (h).

opus.w: This section makes Foreign Service officers on mandatory home leave eligible to use military lodging. It also adds definitions and an effective date. That is eligibility for a benefit, and it goes to federal employees. No one outside the federal government is consulted or given a role in any federal decision. The permissive word "may" refers to the benefit, not to any authority to issue regulations or any process that brings in outsiders.
opus.s:
A Foreign Service officer on mandatory home leave 
may be permitted to use military lodging referred to in subsection (h).
opus.b: The tempting reading is that "may be permitted to use military lodging" lets outside parties take part in something. It fails because it only makes Foreign Service officers, who are federal employees, eligible for a benefit. Nothing in the section involves comment periods, rulemaking, hearings, advisory bodies, consultation with outsiders or a right to sue.

qwen_chat.w: This section amends a statute to expand eligibility for military lodging to include Foreign Service officers on mandatory home leave. This is a change in benefit eligibility, not a requirement for public participation or consultation. Foreign Service officers are federal employees, and the definition excludes applications for benefits or internal government coordination.
qwen_chat.s: (f) Eligibility of Foreign Service Officers on Mandatory Home Leave.—A Foreign Service officer on mandatory home leave may be permitted to use military lodging referred to in subsection (h).
qwen_chat.b: Tempting-but-wrong reading: One might argue that allowing Foreign Service officers to use military lodging involves coordination with the Department of State or the officers themselves, constituting participation. However, this is merely an eligibility rule for a benefit (lodging), not a process for outside parties to consult on or influence a federal decision. The definition explicitly excludes applications for benefits. Furthermore, Foreign Service officers are federal employees, so their involvement is internal.
